primary_reviews.rationale: The opener is exactly what the record claims: 1:1 reads wayehi ish echad min-haramatayim, the presentative wayyiqtol-plus-indefinite-subject pattern, and it is the same shape that stands at Judg 13:2. The rear edge is sturdier than the record argues. At 1:9 a wayyiqtol (vattaqom Channah) is immediately followed by we'Eli hakkohen yoshev, waw plus subject plus participle, which seats a previously off-stage participant in front of the coming scene - the disjunctive differentiator this campaign names by name - and WEB opens a fresh paragraph at that same verse. Dropping vv.1-2 as a standalone pedigree is rightly refused; the son-of chain has no closing register formula and 1:3 continues with we'alah, an iterative weqatal that keeps the same exposition running. I separately probed 1:3|1:4, where wayehi hayyom offers a temporal onset, but neither cast nor place moves across it, so it stays a bare marker and cannot carry a seam on its own. Medium understates a well-anchored unit rather than overstating it.

The 'there was a certain man' formula (vayehi ish echad) that opens the span is the same existential-narrative opener later reused almost verbatim at 9:1 for Kish, which supports reading it as a recognized type-scene launcher rather than an imposed label. The closing edge at v.8 is defensible as a suspended rhetorical question: Elkanah's 'Am I not better to you than ten sons?' never receives a spoken answer anywhere in the text, and the next unit answers it only in action (Hannah rises and prays), which is a slightly different closural mechanism than the location shift the rationale leans on but a real one. The rejected alternative (splitting off vv.1-2 as a bare genealogical notice) is rightly declined, since the two-wife exposition and the rivalry material share unbroken subject continuity.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both primaries land on supports and my own pass through 1:1-1:8 agrees. The vayehi ish echad opener does the work OL claims: it is the same presentative pattern as Judg 13:2 and, notably, gets reused for Kish at 9:1, which both reviewers independently flag from opposite ends of the book and which strengthens the type-scene reading beyond what either alone establishes. OL's rear-edge reinforcement (the disjunctive we-Eli hakkohen yoshev seating a previously off-stage participant at 1:9) is a real addition to LF's rhetorical-question closural argument, not a competing account -- the two operate at different levels (participant-entry vs. unanswered-speech-act) and both hold. No factual error surfaced in either primary's Hebrew or English citations.

primary_reviews.rationale: The isolation of this verse is defensible but the reason given for it is false. The record calls 2:11 a resumptive repetition of 1:28's closing notice and quotes 'the child served Yahweh before Eli the priest' as the thing being resumed. That clause is not in 1:28. I sliced 1:28 directly: it ends vegam anochi hish'iltihu laYHWH ... vayyishtachu sham laYHWH, and a programmatic scan confirms the verse contains neither the root sh-r-t nor the name Eli anywhere in it. So the cited cross-reference at 1:28 supports nothing, and the whole Wiederaufnahme argument collapses with it. What actually justifies a standalone bridge here is a two-clause hinge: a wayyiqtol that closes the Shiloh visit (vayyelech Elqanah haramatah al beito) followed by a disjunctive waw-plus-subject-plus-participle that opens the boy's ongoing service and seeds the refrain later picked up at 2:18, 2:21b and 2:26. The boundary_evidence_ref 'web:1Sam.1.28' therefore points at a verse that does not support the claim made from it.

primary_reviews.rationale: The one-verse bridge function is real and worth keeping as its own unit, but the citation supporting it needs correction. The rationale quotes 'the child served Yahweh before Eli the priest' and attributes that wording to 1:28's closing notice; in fact 1:28 ends with 'he worshiped Yahweh there' and contains no reference to serving or to Eli at all. The quoted phrase is 2:11's own language, and its genuine near-verbatim echo lies downstream at 3:1a ('the boy Samuel was ministering to Yahweh before Eli') with a partial echo upstream at 2:18 ('Samuel ministered before Yahweh... a boy girded with a linen ephod'). Read this way, 2:11, 2:18, and 3:1 form a three-point 'ministering' refrain that literally brackets the entire Eli's-sons corruption complex, running in parallel to the separately-tracked 'growth' refrain at 2:21/2:26 -- a stronger and more structurally significant observation than the current rationale makes, and one the boundary_evidence_refs do not capture.

primary_reviews.rationale: The head of this unit is sound. 2:12 reads uvenei Eli benei veliyya'al, waw plus a subject noun phrase with no finite verb, a genuine disjunctive nominal opening that installs new participants, and the clean text starts a paragraph there. The tail is the problem. 2:15 begins gam beterem yaqtirun et-hachelev, and gam is an additive particle: it marks the next item in the same habitual description rather than a break away from it. The verbal texture confirms this - 2:13-14 run on iterative forms (uva, vehikkah, yiqqach, ya'asu) and 2:15 continues in exactly the same mode with uva na'ar hakkohen ve'amar, so no register shift occurs at that point. WEB agrees: there is no paragraph split before 2:15, and the next one falls at 2:16. The record's own rejected alternative - running through 2:17 as a single custom description - is the reading the Hebrew actually supports. A secondary defect: the rejected-alternative field splices 'Give meat to roast... or I will take it by force' as though it were one utterance, but the first half is the servant's demand at 2:15 and the second half is his rejoinder at 2:16 after the sacrificer objects, two turns with the layman's speech between them.

challenges.claim: The closing edge at 2:14|2:15 cuts against an explicit continuity signal. 2:15 opens with the additive particle gam (gam beterem yaqtirun et-hachelev) and keeps the same iterative verb pattern as 2:13-14, so the priests' custom is still being described, not escalated into a new register; WEB places no paragraph break before 2:15. The seizure language the record uses to justify the split ('I will take it by force') belongs to 2:16, not 2:15, and the rejected-alternative field quotes 2:15 and 2:16 spliced into a single utterance when they are separated by the sacrificer's objection.

The iterative characterisation of 2:13-15 holds on verb morphology: weqatal וּבָ֨א and וְהִכָּ֨ה with yiqtol יַעֲלֶ֣ה, יִקַּ֥ח, יַעֲשׂ֣וּ, then 2:15's גַּם֮ בְּטֶרֶם֮ resuming the same weqatal pattern with וּבָ֣א ... וְאָמַר֙. primary_reviews.rationale: Both flanks check out. At the head, uShemu'el mesharet et penei YHWH is waw plus subject plus participle with no finite verb, so the contrastive force the record calls adversative is carried by the clause type itself and not merely by the rendering's 'But.' The interior is homogeneous durative material: ume'il qaton ta'aseh lo immo with the iterative miyyamim yamimah, then Eli's blessing in 2:20, then the birth summary. The tail sits on vayyigdal hanna'ar Shemu'el im YHWH, and the following verse restarts with the disjunctive we'Eli zaqen me'od, a fresh nominal clause. The traditional division independently sites a samekh after 2:21, which corroborates this rear edge, though only weakly and not as a lifter. The rejected isolation of Eli's blessing is properly refused: 2:20 has no opening or closing formula of its own and its final clause, vehalechu limqomo, hands straight back to the annual-visit frame. The record's forward pointer to a refrain 'recurring' at 2:26 is fair as stated here; the sharper overstatement of that relationship appears at M8-1Sam-012.

The adversative 'but Samuel ministered' opens a genuine contrast panel, and the growth notice closing v.21 ('the child Samuel grew before Yahweh') checks out in Hebrew as a near-exact match for the refrain restated at v.26, so the rationale's forward pointer to v.26 is accurate rather than speculative. Isolating Eli's blessing (v.20) as its own unit is rightly declined, since it sits inside one continuous notice about the family's yearly visits with no independent opening or closing formula of its own.

primary_reviews.rationale: Isolating this verse is a reasonable move and its edges are attested - paragraphs open at 2:26 and 2:27 in the clean text, and a samekh is sited after 2:26 - but the single argument the record offers for the isolation does not survive collation. It says 2:26 restates 2:21b 'almost word for word.' Laid side by side under NFC, 2:21b reads vayyigdal hanna'ar Shemu'el im YHWH and 2:26 reads vehanna'ar Shemu'el holech vegadel vatov gam im YHWH vegam im anashim. The shared material is hanna'ar Shemu'el, the root g-d-l and the phrase im YHWH. Everything else differs: a wayyiqtol in the earlier verse against a disjunctive waw plus subject plus two participles in the later one, plus two elements present only at 2:26 (vatov, and the second gam clause extending favour to human beings). That is a recognisable refrain relationship, not near-verbatim repetition, and the difference matters because a verbatim echo would be the strongest available warrant for a one-verse unit while a loose refrain is a weaker one. The real ground for isolating 2:26 is its clause type - a disjunctive nominal that belongs to neither the confrontation before it nor the messenger speech after it.

challenges.claim: The claim that 2:26 restates 2:21b 'almost word for word' is not accurate. 2:21b is vayyigdal hanna'ar Shemu'el im YHWH (wayyiqtol); 2:26 is vehanna'ar Shemu'el holech vegadel vatov gam im YHWH vegam im anashim (disjunctive waw + subject + participial chain, with vatov and the second gam clause added). They share only hanna'ar Shemu'el, the root g-d-l, and im YHWH. The same overstatement is repeated in the strongest_rejected_alternative field of M8-1Sam-011 ('an almost verbatim repeat of v.21b').
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the evidence for M8-1Sam-012 as a refrain-and-variation relationship rather than near-verbatim repetition, and rest the one-verse isolation on the verse's disjunctive nominal clause type, which attaches it to neither neighbour. Treating this verse as belonging with the following oracle unit is rightly declined: its vocabulary and content stay entirely inside the growth-notice pattern, while the oracle's own messenger formula begins fresh at v.27 with no shared language.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL's challenge is correct and, notably, it contradicts LF's own affirmative position on this exact point -- LF's cluster review calls the restatement 'genuinely close to verbatim,' while OL's side-by-side collation shows otherwise. Laid next to each other, 2:21b (vayyigdal hanna'ar Shemuel im YHWH, a single wayyiqtol) and 2:26 (vehanna'ar Shemuel holekh vegadel vatov gam im YHWH vegam im anashim, a disjunctive waw-subject-participle chain with two elements, vatov and the second gam clause, that 2:21b simply does not have) share only hanna'ar Shemuel, the g-d-l root, and im YHWH -- roughly half the verse's material, in a different verb form. That is a real refrain-with-variation, not near-verbatim repetition, and the distinction matters precisely because the campaign treats verbatim echo as a stronger warrant than a loose refrain. I side with OL against LF's own stated position here: the one-verse isolation should rest on 2:26's disjunctive nominal clause type, which attaches it to neither neighbor, rather than on an overstated repetition claim.

primary_reviews.rationale: The head of this unit is fine - a disjunctive nominal clause on a new topic after the oracle, with a paragraph start in the clean text. The tail is where I cannot affirm the span as drawn, and the reason is syntactic. 3:2 opens vayehi bayyom hahu and then suspends the sentence across a chain of circumstantial clauses: we'Eli shochev bimqomo, ve'einav hechellu chehot, vener Elohim terem yichbeh, uShemu'el shochev beheichal YHWH. None of these completes the period. The main verb arrives only at 3:4 with vayyiqra YHWH el Shemu'el. Cutting between 3:3 and 3:4 therefore severs a protasis from its apodosis. The rendering makes the same structure visible in its punctuation, since 3:2 and 3:3 both end in commas and the sentence closes only at 3:4. The record's rejected alternative asks whether the unit should have been extended to include the first call, but treats it as a register question rather than a syntactic one and dismisses it on that basis. There is also an untested split at 3:1|3:2, where panoramic durative material (the word of YHWH was rare 'in those days') gives way to a specific night, with a samekh sited after 3:1 as weak corroboration. Both the actionable remedy and the confidence question are filed at M8-1Sam-015.

The participial and circumstantial register (Eli laid down, his eyes growing dim, the lamp not yet out, Samuel lying in the temple) is genuinely distinct in kind from the direct-speech call sequence beginning at v.4. This scene-setting cluster also opens with the na'ar-meshareth language that continues the ministering refrain from 2:11/2:18, which is worth noting for anyone tracking that refrain across the chapter break, though it does not change the boundary call here.

Codepoint comparison on the two Hebrew citations came back clean. The register argument for isolating 3:1 is carried by clause form, which I checked directly: the verse consists of two consecutive off-chain clauses, וְהַנַּ֧עַר שְׁמוּאֵ֛ל מְשָׁרֵ֥ת (waw plus NP plus participle) and וּדְבַר יְהוָ֗ה הָיָ֤ה יָקָר֙ (waw plus NP plus qatal), closing on verbless אֵ֥ין חָז֖וֹן נִפְרָֽץ; nothing in the verse sits on the narrative wayyiqtol chain. What follows at 3:2 is וַֽיְהִי֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא, a dated temporal formula, so shrinking the span from 3:1-3:3 to 3:1 alone puts the cut at a real durative-to-dated boundary instead of mid-staging. The parashah file sites a samekh after 3:1 in both witnesses, and the row correctly weights it as weak Prophets-book corroboration rather than as the reason for the span. Retaining medium is right, because 3:1a is simultaneously a Wiederaufnahme of 2:11b and 2:18 and so is tied backward about as firmly as its era-notice register sets it apart.

oshb 3:1 and 3:2 citations verified exact; samekh after 3:1 confirmed in parashah data. The register argument -- a durative, era-level notice (3:1) standing apart from the specific-night frame opened by 3:2's 'vayehi bayom hahu' -- is a sound literary-form distinction, consistent with how the campaign treats other durative summary notices elsewhere in the book. Medium confidence, backed only by weak samekh corroboration, is appropriately calibrated rather than overclaimed.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: I only partly sustain OL's insufficient_evidence flag here. The syntactic observation is accurate as far as it goes -- 3:2 opens vayehi bayyom hahu and runs a chain of circumstantial clauses (we-Eli shochev bimqomo, ve'einav hechellu chehot, vener Elohim terem yichbeh, uShemuel shochev beheichal YHWH) before the first wayyiqtol main verb of the pericope, vayyiqra YHWH el Shemuel, arrives at 3:4. But I do not think this amounts to severing a single unfinished sentence in the strict sense OL's 'syntactic period' language implies: waw-plus-subject-plus-participle clauses of this shape function in Biblical Hebrew narrative as independent backgrounding clauses, not as subordinate elements that grammatically require the following wayyiqtol to complete them. What is real and does weaken the current cut is that 3:4 supplies a genuine register shift -- from circumstantial description into the first direct-speech exchange of the chapter -- which is a stronger, more defensible driving signal than the weak pe sited after 3:3 that the rationale leans on without naming. I'd ask for the rationale to cite that register shift explicitly rather than relying implicitly on the pe mark, while disclosing OL's 3:1|3:2 alternative (addressed fully at 015) as a live competing reading.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both quotations verify against WEB, and the record's identification of the closing device is a genuinely good original-language observation: 3:14 reads velachen nishba'ti leveit Eli im yitkapper avon beit Eli bezevach uveminchah ad olam, where nishba'ti governs an im clause with the standard negative oath force, so calling it an oath formula is exact rather than impressionistic. The rear edge is firmer - 3:15 turns on a wayyiqtol with a jump to morning and a disjunctive uShemu'el yare mehaggid, and the clean text opens a paragraph there. Rejecting a merger with the call type-scene is correct given that the pattern reaches its own resolution at 3:10.

Yahweh's direct address runs as one uninterrupted oracle from 'Behold, I will do a thing in Israel' through the oath formula 'the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be removed... forever,' with no renewed speech-formula or narrative interruption in between, so a single span is correct. The opening edge against the type-scene's own closural 'Speak; for your servant hears' (v.10) is a clean formula-to-formula transition rather than an inferred one.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Supports on both sides, no dispute. Both reviewers verify the oath-formula quotation (nishba'ti... im yitkapper) accurately.

primary_reviews.rationale: Verified oshb 3:19, 3:21, and 4:1 citations exact, and independently confirmed by direct re-parse of 1Sam_web_clean.txt that WEB's paragraph break genuinely falls mid-verse inside 4:1 -- after the devar-clause ('the word of Samuel came to all Israel') and before 'Israel went out against the Philistines' -- a real, verified signal, not an artifact of my own initial (buggy) parse. The tag correction is correct: 3:19-21 has no age-at-accession or reign-length clause, unlike 13:1's genuine two-clause accession formula. This is the most methodologically careful decision in the cluster: rather than forcing a boundary, it honestly discloses the 4:1a Janus-facing tension (bound backward by register/catchword, forward by an unbroken wayyiqtol chain with no disjunctive marker) as a live, unresolved alternative. Downgrade to medium is earned.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: The row's own Janus-faced disclosure of 4:1a is honest work -- it doesn't silently pick a side -- but ROL-018-1 catches a real asymmetry in how the two pulls are described. The devar-catchword pull backward is argued carefully (shared vocabulary, WEB's own mid-verse paragraph break). The wayyiqtol-chain pull forward is asserted flatly ('unbroken...with no disjunctive marker') without noting that the second verb, vayyetse, names its subject explicitly (Yisra'el) rather than continuing on an implicit one. Other decisions in this book that invoke subject-fronting or explicit-subject reintroduction (045's 9:5 hemmah ba'u, 057's vehinneh Sha'ul ba) treat it as a signal of its own, so treating 4:1a's named-subject wayyiqtol as equivalent in strength to a bare one is an inconsistency within the row's own toolkit, not just an omission.

peer_crosscheck_history.assessment: I find the underlying observation shared by both sides is correct but I favor OL's fallback remedy over an outright span extension. 4:1a is genuinely Janus-faced: backward, it shares the devar catchword and the durative, all-Israel register with 3:19 and 3:21 (a pattern LF names but files as a disclosure request at 019 rather than a direct challenge here); forward, it is bound to 4:1b by a plain wayyiqtol chain (vayehi devar Shemuel lechol Yisrael vayetze Yisrael) with no disjunctive marker at all, which is itself a real continuity signal pulling toward the battle narrative. OL adds that WEB's own paragraph break falls inside 4:1, after the devar clause, which if accurate would mean the substrate this campaign privileges disagrees with the drafted cut rather than merely failing to support it. Given that the grammar genuinely pulls in both directions, I do not think either placement is provably 'more correct' than the other, so I prefer disclosure-plus-downgrade over a mandated chapter-crossing extension: keep the span at 3:19-3:21 but drop from high to medium, and record the devar-chain reading as the live, unresolved alternative in both this decision and 019.

primary_reviews.rationale: I can affirm the rear edge but not the front. At the rear, 4:3 opens vayyavo ha'am el hammachaneh, a wayyiqtol with a move into the camp, and the elders then take the subject slot; the record's description of a separate deliberation scene is accurate. At the front, the record itself calls vayehi devar Shemu'el lechol Yisra'el 'a hinge' and then attaches it forward without recording why forward rather than backward. The substrate points backward: the clean text breaks paragraph inside 4:1 immediately after that clause, and the clause matches 3:19-21 in register, scope and vocabulary. The strongest_rejected_alternative field engages a different and weaker question - whether the pair should absorb the council scene - and so never tests the live one. The traditional division sites a pe after 3:21, which favours the decision as drawn, but weak corroboration cannot settle the point by itself. The actionable remedy sits at OL-M8-1Sam-018-1; I record the deficiency here rather than duplicating the challenge.

The casualty-count closing edge is solid and uncontested. The opening-edge claim is more debatable than the rationale allows: 4:1a ('the word of Samuel came to all Israel') shares its key noun -- devar, 'word' -- with the two closing verses of the immediately preceding regnal-summary unit (3:19's 'let none of his devarav fall to the ground,' 3:21's 'by the devar of Yahweh'), and Hebrew joins 4:1a to 4:1b with a plain narrative vav-consecutive chain (vayehi...vayetze) rather than any disjunctive marker. A reasonable alternative reading treats 4:1a as the capstone of the prophetic-establishment summary (3:19-4:1a) on the strength of that lexical chain, rather than as the opening hinge of the battle narrative the rationale assigns it to. This is offered as a live alternative worth disclosing rather than a certain correction, since the grammar alone does not decide it either way.

challenges.issue: The rationale treats 4:1a as opening the battle narrative without weighing an alternative reading in which it closes the preceding prophetic-establishment summary (3:19-21), on the strength of a shared davar root running across 3:19, 3:21, and 4:1a.

primary_reviews.rationale: The stated closing evidence misreports what 4:4 narrates. The record says the unit 'closes when the ark and Eli's two sons arrive at the camp.' The verse says vayyishlach ha'am Shiloh vayyis'u misham et aron berit YHWH tseva'ot yoshev hakeruvim, with the disjunctive tail vesham shenei venei Eli - the people send to Shiloh, the ark is carried out from there, and the sons are noted as being there, at Shiloh, alongside it. Nothing has reached the camp. The arrival is narrated in the next verse, vayehi kevo aron berit YHWH el hammachaneh, which the decision assigns to a different unit. Since arrival is the event on which the rear edge is said to close, the error is load-bearing. There is a second problem at the front: the clean text starts a paragraph at 4:4, so the ¶ metadata groups 4:3 with the battle report before it and begins fresh where this unit is already underway. What genuinely separates 4:4 from 4:5 is the change of narrative vantage from the dispatching party to the camp receiving the ark, and that should be stated instead. primary_reviews.rationale: The one-verse unit is defensible on its clause type - vachamishah sarnei Pelishtim ra'u vayyashuvu Eqron bayyom hahu is waw plus subject plus qatal, a disjunctive that steps aside from the Beth Shemesh action to close out the Philistine side, and it is followed at 6:17 by an enumerative formula and shadowed by a samekh sited after 6:16. But the justification the record gives for it is demonstrably false. It asserts that 'the lords have not been narrative subjects since chapter 5,' and cites 5:11. Four verses earlier, at 6:12, the text reads vesarnei Pelishtim holechim achareihem ad gevul Beit Shamesh: the lords are the explicit subject of a disjunctive clause following the cart to the border of Beth Shemesh. They are also named inside the counsel at 6:4. So they have been on stage continuously through the cart sequence, and their appearance at 6:16 is not a reappearance after an absence but the resolution of a role they have been holding since 6:12. That matters because the asserted absence is the entire basis for calling this 'a genuine if brief participant shift.' The verse can still be isolated, but on the disjunctive construction and the enumerative formula that follows it, not on a gap that does not exist.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two independent problems, both of which bear on the high rating and on the list_register tag. First, the span and its stated opening do not match. The record says the unit opens on the introductory formula 'This will be the way of the king,' but that formula is 8:11 (vayyomer zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelech asher yimloch aleichem). The span's actual first verse, 8:10, is narrative: vayyomer Shemu'el et kol divrei YHWH el ha'am hasho'alim me'itto melech - a report that Samuel relayed the words, containing no enumeration at all. So the catalog is tagged as beginning one verse before it begins, and the samekh sited after 8:10 gives weak corroboration that 8:10 stands apart. Second, the anaphora claim does not survive the Hebrew. The record says 'He will take' runs uniformly across all nine verses 'without any internal formula change.' In fact the fronted-object plus yiqqach pattern appears at 8:11, 8:13, 8:14 and 8:16, while 8:15 and 8:17 use a different verb, ya'sor (he will tithe), 8:12 has no finite verb of taking at all (velasum lo sarei alafim), and 8:18 breaks the pattern completely by switching to second person, uze'aqtem bayyom hahu. The apparent uniformity is a product of WEB rendering ya'sor as 'He will take one tenth of', which is precisely the kind of translation-side flattening an original-language check exists to catch.

challenges.claim: The span begins one verse before the formula the rationale cites as its opening edge. 1Sam.8.10 is narrative report (vayyomer Shemu'el et kol divrei YHWH el ha'am hasho'alim me'itto melech); the introductory formula zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelech is 8:11. WEB renders ya'sor as 'He will take one tenth of', which manufactures the uniformity the rationale relies on.

primary_reviews.rationale: The seven Hebrew citations survive a codepoint diff intact, and I independently tested the row's central morphological claim across the verses it does not quote. The fronted-object-plus-yiqqach pattern is present at all four verses named and nowhere else: אֶת בְּנֵיכֶ֣ם יִקָּ֗ח (8:11), וְאֶת בְּנוֹתֵיכֶ֖ם יִקָּ֑ח (8:13), וְאֶת שְׂ֠דֽוֹתֵיכֶם ... יִקָּ֑ח (8:14) and וְאֶת עַבְדֵיכֶם֩ ... יִקָּ֑ח (8:16); the alternating verb is יַעְשֹׂ֑ר at 8:15 and 8:17; 8:12 carries only infinitives (וְלָשׂ֣וּם, וְלַחֲרֹ֤שׁ, וְלִקְצֹ֣ר, וְלַעֲשׂ֥וֹת) and no finite taking verb. So the correction from 'uniform anaphora' to a two-verb alternation is exactly right, and the withdrawal of the WEB-driven uniformity is well judged. The moved front edge is the strongest point: 8:10 is narratorial report with no enumeration, while 8:11 supplies the catalogue's own formula, וַיֹּ֕אמֶר זֶ֗ה יִֽהְיֶה֙ מִשְׁפַּ֣ט הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ. The rear edge is equally clean, with 8:18's second-plural weqatal וּזְעַקְתֶּם֙ breaking the pattern and 8:19's וַיְמָאֲנ֣וּ הָעָ֔ם resuming narration. Both cited samekh sites are attested in both witnesses and are held at weak weight throughout.

Verified the two-verb-alternation claim verse-by-verse against oshb: fronted-object-plus-yiqqach at 8:11, 8:13, 8:14, and 8:16; no finite taking verb at 8:12 (infinitives lasum/lacharosh/vela'asot only); the distinct verb ya'sor at 8:15 and 8:17; and the pattern-breaking second-person consequence clause at 8:18 ('uze'aqtem'). Every element of this claim is exactly correct against the Hebrew. The introductory-formula argument (8:11's 'zeh yihyeh mishpat hamelekh' vs. 8:10's narratorial report with no enumeration) is sound, and samekh after both 8:9 and 8:10 is confirmed in parashah_two_witness.json. A precise, rigorously verified philological argument; high confidence is fully earned.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the strongest convergent-plus-additive finding in the range and all three challenges verify against direct collation. On the off-by-one opener, 8:10 (vayyomer Shemuel et kol divrei YHWH el ha'am hasho'alim me'itto melech) is narrative report with no enumeration at all; the introductory formula zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelech the rationale quotes as the span's opener is 8:11's language, one verse later -- LF and OL caught this independently and agree exactly. On the anaphora, OL's deeper Hebrew-grain check overturns a claim LF's own review affirmatively endorsed: LF states the 'He will take' structure 'runs uniformly across all of them without any internal formula change,' but collation shows the fronted-object-plus-yiqqach pattern only at 8:11, 8:13, 8:14, and 8:16, while 8:15 and 8:17 use the distinct verb ya'sor ('he will tithe'), 8:12 has no finite taking verb at all (velasum lo sarei alafim), and 8:18 shifts to second person entirely (uze'aqtem bayyom hahu). WEB's rendering of ya'sor as 'he will take one tenth of' is exactly the kind of translation-side flattening that manufactures the false uniformity LF's review relies on -- so on this specific sub-point, LF's own assessment is superseded and OL's correction should be treated as the operative one. I recommend re-cutting the span to open at 8:11 (attaching 8:10 to 041 as the narrative discharge of Yahweh's instruction, or leaving it as a standalone hinge notice) and restating the interior evidence as a two-verb alternation resolving to a second-person consequence clause, rather than as uniform anaphora.

primary_reviews.rationale: The refusal genuinely does reopen narrated dialogue after the catalog: vayema'anu ha'am lishmoa beqol Shemu'el vayyomeru lo ki im melech yihyeh aleinu, a wayyiqtol pair with the people taking the subject slot back, and a paragraph starts there. The unit then runs through Samuel's report to Yahweh at 8:21 and the instruction and dismissal at 8:22, closing the sequence and the chapter. The rear edge is firm because 9:1 opens a new presentative sentence with a new cast, and a pe is sited after 8:22. Refusing to peel the dismissal off as a coda is right on the plain grammar - the instruction and Samuel's compliance sit in the same verse with nothing between them - and I note that the tradition sites a pe after 8:21 as well, which would isolate 8:22 entirely; weak corroboration for the rejected reading, and not a lifter, so the decision stands. There is also a pe after 8:3 and one after 8:6 in this chapter, so the traditional divisions here are dense and consistently finer-grained than the draft's; that pattern is worth carrying forward but cannot drive anything.

The people's refusal and repeated demand genuinely reopen dialogue after the catalog's register closes, and treating Samuel's dismissal (v.22b) as the direct, same-verse continuation of Yahweh's instruction rather than its own coda respects that there is no scene gap between the command and the compliance.

primary_reviews.rationale: The type-scene opening is bounded soundly. On the focus test's framing I should be precise: 9:1 is not a disjunctive clause. It reads vayehi ish mibbinyamin usmo Qish, a presentative wayyiqtol with an indefinite subject - formally the same opener as 1:1's vayehi ish echad - so the front edge is a presentative formula reinforced by the pe sited after 8:22 and a paragraph start, not a waw-x construction. The son-of chain that follows is genuine register form, and 'five-generation' is a fair count (Kish, Abiel, Zeror, Becorath, Aphiah) before the generic ben ish yemini and the epithet gibbor chayil. The rear edge holds on the turn from static description to event at 9:3, vattovadnah ha'atonot leQish, with a paragraph opening there. Content-vs-tag note: 9:2 is character description rather than genealogy proper (bachur vatov, taller than any of the people), so the genealogical_register tag covers 9:1 exactly and 9:2 by extension. The ketiv/qere at 9:1 is printed as mbn ymyn written against mibbinyamin read; it bears on nothing here and is noted as inspected.

primary_reviews.rationale: High confidence is earned on independent grounds at both edges. Opening: Mizpah is a new location, 'all Israel' a new participant-scope, and the rebuke-oracle a new register against the private uncle-scene just closed -- three converging signals, not one. Closing: the acclamation formula 'Long live the king!' is a natural climax, and v.25 pivots to administrative content (recording, writing in a book, dismissal) in a way that is a real register shift, not merely a topic drift. The refusal to split the rebuke-speech from the lottery is correct: this is one national-assembly type-scene (summons, accusatory address, then the sacred lot performed by the very assembly just addressed), structurally cousin to the tribe-clan-household-man narrowing at Josh 7's Achan lot. That same narrowing-by-elimination shape recurs twice more within this reviewer's own assigned range -- at 14:36-42 (the lot that isolates Jonathan) and again, in a different mechanism, at 16:6-10's parade-elimination of Jesse's sons -- forming a three-fold structural rhyme across chs. 10-16 worth flagging as a cluster-spanning literary-form finding, not merely local to this one span.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Jabesh material is one of the clearer episodes in the book and I have no quarrel with treating it as several units. The quarrel is with where the first cut falls. Verse 3 ends with the elders proposing to dispatch runners, וְנִשְׁלְחָה֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל, and verse 4 executes that proposal in the flattest possible way, וַיָּבֹ֤אוּ הַמַּלְאָכִים֙ גִּבְעַ֣ת שָׁא֔וּל, wayyiqtol plus the definite noun the previous verse just supplied. Cutting there separates a plan from its immediate discharge and does so at a marker that recurs everywhere. One verse later the narrator supplies precisely the construction that a scene change wants: וְהִנֵּ֣ה שָׁא֗וּל בָּ֣א אַחֲרֵ֤י הַבָּקָר֙ מִן הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה, waw plus presentative plus named subject plus participle, entirely off the narrative chain, walking onto the page a figure who has not appeared since the previous chapter closed. That is the only such clause in chapter 11. The drafted arrangement buries it in the middle of the following unit, whose own rationale notices it as a striking detail without drawing the structural consequence. The record has the right observation attached to the wrong seam.

primary_reviews.rationale: Codepoint comparison on the four Hebrew citations came back clean, and I tested the row's strongest claim exhaustively rather than accepting it: I scanned every verse of 1 Samuel 11 in OSHB for a hinneh construction, and 11:5's וְהִנֵּ֣ה שָׁא֗וּל בָּ֣א אַחֲרֵ֤י הַבָּקָר֙ מִן הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה is indeed the only one in the chapter. The anaphora argument for absorbing 11:4 also holds on the article: 11:3 proposes indefinite מַלְאָכִ֔ים and 11:4 discharges it with definite הַמַּלְאָכִים֙, so 11:4 completes a plan rather than opening a scene, and the waw-presentative that actually re-introduces an absent participant sits one verse further on. Moving the edge to 11:4|11:5 is therefore better grounded than the drafted 11:3|11:4. Two evidence entries record the absence of parashah marks after 11:3 and 11:4; they are inert under the binding rules and, to the row's credit, the rationale does not argue from them. That said, this is a defensible-but-not-mandatory alternative rather than a missed seam: unlike, say, 12:1-3/12:4-5, none of the candidate sub-boundaries here is marked by a genuine function shift (challenge-to-verdict) as opposed to mere narrative continuation toward a single outcome, so I do not raise this to a challenge. Also worth noting for texture: Jabesh's own promise to Nahash, 'Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us all that seems good to you,' is a nice piece of dramatic irony -- it reads to Nahash as capitulation but is, to the reader who already knows the rescue is coming, literally true.

primary_reviews.rationale: Medium is well judged for a span whose edges are of unequal strength. The far edge is beyond dispute: 11:15 ends the chapter on massed rejoicing, וַיִּשְׂמַ֨ח שָׁ֥ם שָׁא֛וּל וְכָל אַנְשֵׁ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עַד מְאֹֽד, both witnesses mark a pe there, and 12:1 opens a formal address to all Israel. The near edge is a speech turn, though an unusually loaded one, since verse 12 changes both speaker and addressee at once, the people turning to Samuel rather than to the king they have just followed into battle. On the rejected alternative I agree with the outcome, though on evidence the record never cites. A samekh does fall after 11:13, exactly where the rejected split would go, between the clemency ruling and Samuel's call to Gilgal, so the tradition is not silent about that seam. Under the Prophets weighting it corroborates weakly at best and cannot lift a boundary, and the text signal points the other way: 11:14 opens with an ordinary speech formula and the crowd never disperses between the ruling and the renewal. The merge is correct; it should just be recorded as reached against a tradition mark rather than in the absence of one.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges confirmed: v.12's post-victory demand for execution opens a new beat after the battle notice closes at v.11, and 12:1's fresh, formal 'Samuel said to all Israel' address opens a wholly different speech-register (farewell address) against this chapter's narrative close. One clean royal-speech form worth naming: 'No man shall be put to death today; for today Yahweh has rescued Israel' is a formal clemency pronouncement (grounds given, verdict stated, in that order), a recognizable subtype distinct from Nahash's threat-speech and from Samuel's later covenant-lawsuit register, and its presence here usefully varies the register texture of the chapter.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the row the recalibration already demoted, and my reading is that demotion did not go far enough, because the problem is not the price but the seam. Chapter 12 verses 1 to 6 present five consecutive quoted turns, each introduced by the same verb: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל at verse 1, וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ at verse 4, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֜ם and then a second וַיֹּ֖אמֶר inside verse 5, and וַיֹּ֥אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל אֶל הָעָ֑ם at verse 6. The draft cuts before the second of these and before the fifth, and treats the third and fourth as internal. Nothing in the morphology distinguishes them. The warrant offered is a shift of rhetorical function from accusation-invitation to formal verdict, which is an interpretive category rather than a text signal, and the campaign's own turn-marker principle exists precisely to stop that category from generating seams. primary_reviews.rationale: This is the flagged internal split (12:1-3 | 12:4-5) and I do not think it survives the campaign's own turn-marker principle as cleanly as the boundary_rationale claims. The rationale's argument is that the shift from 'accusation-invitation' (vv.1-3) to 'formal verdict' (vv.4-5) is a genuine rhetorical-function change, not a bare turn. But read as a whole, 12:1-5 is a single, tightly bound legal ritual: Samuel issues a challenge inviting testimony against himself (vv.1-3), the people supply exactly the testimony he solicited (v.4 -- this is not an independent speech-act, it is the very response the challenge was structured to elicit), and Samuel then seals the outcome with a formal double-witness formula that the people themselves confirm (v.5, 'He is witness'). That is one call-and-response oath-of-clearance scene with an internal witness-sealing coda, structurally closer to the campaign's own precedent at 1:9-18 (the Hannah-Eli exchange, kept as one span across three speech turns because no scene or topic changed) than to a genuine two-part covenant-lawsuit movement. Compare also M8-1Sam-069 in this reviewer's range, where Saul's excuse and Samuel's rebuke are correctly kept together as 'one uninterrupted exchange' despite being two speakers with two different rhetorical postures (self-justification vs. verdict) -- the same logic, applied consistently, would seem to favor holding 12:1-5 together rather than splitting at v.3/v.4. There is also a small piece of weak, non-driving corroboration worth surfacing: per parashah_two_witness.json, the Masoretic pe mark falls after 12:5, not after 12:3 -- the traditional paragraphing apparatus (weak, PROPHETS-book corroboration only, per the file's own caveat) marks a unit boundary at the end of the whole exchange, not mid-exchange. This does not prove the split is wrong on its own, but it is available evidence that was left on the table and points the same direction as the turn-marker concern.

primary_reviews.rationale: A high grade on a form-critical unit invites form-critical checking, and the span does not survive it intact. Two objections, both about where the recital actually begins and ends. At the near end, verse 6 is a nominal predication about Yahweh and verse 7 is a summons, וְעַתָּ֗ה הִֽתְיַצְּב֛וּ וְאִשָּׁפְטָ֥ה אִתְּכֶ֖ם לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה, with the reflexive imperative and the cohortative of judgment that mark the opening move of a suit. The recital proper starts only at verse 8, whose first words are כַּֽאֲשֶׁר בָּ֥א יַעֲקֹ֖ב מִצְרָ֑יִם. Folding summons and recital into one unit under the single label covenant_lawsuit_speech blurs the two form-elements the label exists to distinguish. At the far end the case is weaker still. primary_reviews.rationale: Medium is correct and I would resist any pressure to raise it, on grounds the record has not registered. The far edge is argued from the imperative that opens 12:16, and that imperative is not new: גַּם עַתָּה֙ הִתְיַצְּב֣וּ וּרְא֔וּ picks up וְעַתָּ֗ה הִֽתְיַצְּב֛וּ from 12:7 with the same verb in the same stem, adding only the intensifying particle. Under the campaign's treatment of resumptive repetition as a binding rather than a dividing device, a clause that reaches back over verses 8 to 15 to rejoin an earlier summons is evidence of continuity across the seam, not of a fresh start. What does mark the transition is the change of mode, from conditional instruction to a demonstrative act with a natural sign attached, and that is a real signal, which is why I do not challenge the span. But the two considerations pull in opposite directions and medium is exactly the price that reflects it. The conditional pair itself is well drawn: אִם תִּֽירְא֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֗ה at 12:14 against וְאִם לֹ֤א תִשְׁמְעוּ֙ at 12:15, protasis answered by protasis, with 12:15 closing the reciprocal on יַד יְהוָ֛ה בָּכֶ֖ם.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the flagged form-judgment test -- does a broken formula still carry its own row -- and the answer is yes, on grounds stronger than the boundary_rationale states. The point that matters for a form judgment is that the damage sits at the level of textual transmission (a lost or corrupted numeral), not at the level of literary form: the verse still parses as a two-clause accession notice and is recognizably in a different register from both the covenant-lawsuit speech that closes at 12:25 and the narrative_prose troop-muster that opens at 13:2 ('Saul chose for himself three thousand men'). A broken numeral inside an intact formula is exactly the kind of case where the form, not the content, should carry the row, and isolating it as its own regnal_summary_notice span is the right call.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the Gilgal rejection scene and the high rating is earned at both edges. Opening: the specific seven-day countdown named in v.8 is genuinely distinct from the general mobilization report that precedes it. Closing: v.14's climactic sentence ('Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart') is a natural peroration, and v.15's fresh action verbs and relocation ('Samuel arose, and went from Gilgal to Gibeah... Saul counted the people') is a clean narrative resumption in a different register. The decision to keep Saul's excuse (vv.11-12) fused with Samuel's rebuke (vv.13-14) as one uninterrupted exchange rather than splitting at the speaker-turn is the correct application of the turn-marker principle: there is no independent scene or topic change between accusation and answer here, unlike the more contestable case flagged at 12:1-3/12:4-5 elsewhere in this reviewer's range. On classification: keeping this narrative_prose rather than tagging it prophetic_oracle_speech is right, since Samuel's rebuke is presented as spontaneous confrontation-dialogue rather than introduced by a messenger/divine-word formula (contrast 15:1-3's explicit 'Thus says Yahweh of Armies' citation) -- the campaign is applying that distinction consistently.

primary_reviews.rationale: Character-level comparison on the five Hebrew citations is clean, and every form-element the retag rests on is present as described. I checked each in turn: 13:19 is a negated durative, וְחָרָשׁ֙ לֹ֣א יִמָּצֵ֔א, with an embedded motive clause of direct speech (כִּֽי אמר אָמְר֣וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים פֶּ֚ן יַעֲשׂ֣וּ, ketiv/qere preserved); 13:20 turns on the purpose infinitive לִ֠לְטוֹשׁ; 13:21 is the pim price notice; 13:22 is a temporal frame, וְהָיָה֙ בְּי֣וֹם מִלְחֶ֔מֶת; and 13:23 resumes the storyline with a wayyiqtol, וַיֵּצֵא֙ מַצַּ֣ב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים אֶֽל מַעֲבַ֖ר מִכְמָֽשׂ. None of that is an enumerated series with a repeated frame, whereas the contrast case is: 13:17 does open a genuine three-member catalogue with שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה רָאשִׁ֑ים הָרֹ֨אשׁ אֶחָ֥ד יִפְנֶ֛ה. The list_register to narrative_prose retag is therefore correct and high confidence is justified. Both cited samekh sites, after 13:18 and after 13:23, are attested in both witnesses and bracket the span. The WEB footnote citation matches the substrate as a truncated prefix (the source continues 'or 0.26 ounces, or 7.6 grams') and is used descriptively only, not as a boundary driver.

Verified oshb 13:17 and 13:19-13:22 citations exact, and the WEB 13:21 footnote text ('A payim (or pim) was 2/3 shekel of silver...') confirmed present verbatim. The retagging argument holds: 13:19-23 mixes a negated durative statement, a purpose infinitive, an embedded price notice, a temporal frame, and a resuming wayyiqtol -- genuinely heterogeneous forms, not a repeated enumerated frame, unlike the three-member 'ha-rosh' catalog at 13:17. samekh after both 13:18 and 13:23 confirmed. Sound tag correction from list_register to narrative_prose.

primary_reviews.rationale: Medium is conservative and I am content with it, but the edges are firmer than the record says. The unit opens with a dedicated temporal formula, וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֗וֹם, which occurs nowhere else in chapters 13 or 14 and which exists to start a scene. It closes on a disjunctive notice of ignorance, וְהָעָם֙ לֹ֣א יָדַ֔ע כִּ֥י הָלַ֖ךְ יוֹנָתָֽן, and 14:4 then steps off the chain with a fronted prepositional phrase, וּבֵ֣ין הַֽמַּעְבְּר֗וֹת. So both edges carry a construction rather than mere content. The rejected alternative is resolved correctly, and for a reason worth adding: 14:4 and 14:5 are verbless or near-verbless topographic description, הַשֵּׁ֧ן הָאֶחָ֛ד מָצ֥וּק מִצָּפ֖וֹן, a mode that neither 14:1 nor 14:2 shares. One structural observation the record does not make: 14:2 is itself disjunctive and participial, וְשָׁא֗וּל יוֹשֵׁב֙ בִּקְצֵ֣ה הַגִּבְעָ֔ה, so the drafted unit is really Jonathan's proposal plus a parenthesis about Saul, joined rather than continuous. Keeping them together as one scene-setting block is a reasonable call, but it is a call, and the rationale presents it as seamless.

primary_reviews.rationale: The 'vayehi hayom' scene-opener at v.1 is a recognizable Hebrew narrative-launch idiom (cf. 1:4) and marks a strong opening edge; the closing at v.3's dramatic-irony note ('The people didn't know that Jonathan was gone') gives way at v.4 to purely topographical description (named crags) in a different descriptive register, which is a real seam. Worth noting: the embedded priestly genealogy in v.3 (Ahijah, son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli) is not incidental filler -- it quietly signals that the doomed Elide line from the judgment oracle at 2:27-36 is still serving at Saul's camp, which is the kind of thematic anchoring embedded genealogical asides do elsewhere in the book (compare 9:1-2's Kish genealogy and 14:49-51's family register). That reading supports keeping it inside this narrative unit rather than isolating it.

primary_reviews.rationale: The near edge is genuine. 14:4 fronts a prepositional phrase, וּבֵ֣ין הַֽמַּעְבְּר֗וֹת, and 14:4 to 14:5 are verbless topographic description with named crags, a mode nothing before them shares. The far edge is the problem, and it is the same problem the recalibration already identified in chapter 12. Jonathan speaks at 14:6, the armour-bearer answers at 14:7, Jonathan speaks again at 14:8; the draft cuts between the second and third of those turns. Each is introduced by the same verb in the same form, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן, וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֔יו, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן, and neither participant leaves, nothing is narrated between them, and the place does not change. The warrant supplied for the seam is that the pledge is a fitting close and the sign-speech is a new beginning, which is a description of what the speeches are about, not of anything marking them off. A samekh does fall after 14:7, and I record it, but the Prophets weighting makes it weak corroboration that cannot drive a boundary and cannot lift one. The campaign has already declined to price a rhetorical function change as an edge at 12:3/12:4. The same ruling has to reach here, or the principle is not a principle.

challenges.claim: The 14:7/14:8 seam is carried by a symmetric turn marker and is treated inconsistently with the campaign's own handling of 12:3/12:4. Verses 6, 7 and 8 are three turns of one uninterrupted two-party exchange, each opened by an identical speech verb with a named speaker, with no narrated action, no participant change and no change of place between them. The seam therefore rests on a rhetorical distinction between assent and operational plan, which is the same warrant the recalibration rejected in chapter 12. The samekh after 14:7 is weak corroboration under the Prophets weighting and cannot supply what the text signal does not.

primary_reviews.rationale: Topographical notice into the armor-bearer's unconditional pledge is well-bounded, opening on named-crag description (a register shift from the preceding scene-setting) and closing where v.8's 'Then Jonathan said' opens the specific binary sign-proposal in a different, conditional mood. The functional distinction matters here: v.7's pledge is general loyalty ('I am with you according to your heart'), a necessary precondition before Jonathan can propose the concrete sign that follows -- general commitment and specific plan are genuinely different speech-acts, unlike the more contestable turn-split flagged elsewhere in this reviewer's range at 12:1-3/12:4-5, where the second speaker's content was solicited by the first rather than freestanding.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three Hebrew citations survive a codepoint diff intact, and the row's description of the rear edge is accurate in a way that matters: 14:6, 14:7 and 14:8 do each open with a bare wayyomer plus an expressed subject — וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן, וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֔יו, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן — with no narrated action, participant change or relocation between them, so the drafted 14:7|14:8 seam really is a bare speaker change dressed up as a register shift. Naming that honestly and dropping to low is the right call. A samekh after 14:7 is attested in both witnesses, and the row's handling of it is exemplary: it is admitted as weak Prophets-book corroboration and explicitly refused the power to install a boundary the clause structure does not mark, which is precisely what the binding weighting requires. The 073/074 merge is correctly flagged upward rather than executed unilaterally. Note that the front edge at 14:3|14:4 and the topographical notice at 14:4-5 are not evidenced in this row, which the low rating already absorbs.

Verified oshb 14:6-14:8 citations exact -- all three turns (Jonathan's proposal, the armor-bearer's pledge, Jonathan's response) open with a vayomer formula as claimed. samekh after 14:7 confirmed. The self-consistency argument, paralleling the 12:3/12:4 turn-marker finding in M8-1Sam-061, is well-founded, and naming the true edge honestly as 'a bare speaker change' rather than dressing it up as a register shift is the right move -- the downgrade to low confidence matches how thin the actual textual signal is at this seam.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL's challenge is confirmed and is a third instance, alongside M8-1Sam-061 and M8-1Sam-069, of the same recurring defect: a rhetorical or content distinction doing the work a text signal should. 14:6, 14:7, and 14:8 are three turns of one uninterrupted exchange, each opened by the identical formula (וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן / וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֔יו / וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹנָתָ֔ן), with no narrated action, no participant change, and no relocation between them. The samekh after 14:7 is confirmed present but, as OL notes, is weak Prophets-weighted corroboration that cannot itself carry a boundary the text does not otherwise mark. The campaign has already declined to price the assent-versus-plan distinction as an edge at 12:3/12:4 (per M8-1Sam-061 above); consistency requires the same ruling here. I support the challenge and recommend either the 14:4-10 merge OL proposes, letting the genuine mood shift at 14:10/14:11 (conditional speech to indicative fulfillment) carry the far edge, or an explicit re-pricing below medium with the true marker named honestly.

primary_reviews.rationale: On the internal question the row is right, and the Hebrew shows it more cleanly than the argument given. The two defecting groups are not merely similar in content; they are cast in matching syntax, וְהָעִבְרִ֗ים הָי֤וּ לַפְּלִשְׁתִּים֙ at 14:21 and וְכֹל֩ אִ֨ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל הַמִּֽתְחַבְּאִ֤ים at 14:22, each a fronted subject with a following predicate, and each closing with גַם הֵ֗מָּה. Two clauses built to the same template are one movement, so splitting them would be an error. Two corrections. The row treats the notice that Yahweh saved Israel that day as its terminus; that clause is the first half of 14:23, and the verse actually ends with a further disjunctive clause, וְהַ֨מִּלְחָמָ֔ה עָבְרָ֖ה אֶת בֵּ֥ית אָֽוֶן, which moves the action along rather than concluding it. The edge is still sound, since a transitional clause is a serviceable terminus, but the quoted evidence is one clause short of the boundary. Second, the description of the returning Hebrews as mercenaries has no basis in the text, which says only that they had been with the Philistines כְּאֶתְמ֣וֹל שִׁלְשׁ֔וֹם and went up with them.

primary_reviews.rationale: Medium is the ceiling here and the row has found it. The opening is well marked, וְאִֽישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל נִגַּ֖שׂ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא, waw plus fronted subject plus qatal, and the oath and its violation are correctly kept together, since 14:27 states the ignorance and the act in one breath and 14:28 supplies the informant. The closing is the softest edge in the cluster and the record should say so. 14:31 opens with a bare wayyiqtol, וַיַּכּ֞וּ בַּיּ֤וֹם הַהוּא֙, whose temporal phrase repeats the one that opened this very span at 14:24, so the clause reaches back over Jonathan's speech to rejoin the day it began in, which is a binding gesture rather than a dividing one. A methodological note that bears on this whole chapter. Fronted-subject clauses are not distinctive here the way they are elsewhere in the book; 14:21, 14:22, 14:24, 14:25 and 14:27 all use one, so in this stretch the construction is the narrator's default for tracking parallel groups and cannot by itself grade a seam. The record should also know that at 14:27 the consonants ותראנה stand against a reading וַתָּאֹ֖רְנָה, whose root then supplies Jonathan's own כִּֽי אֹ֣רוּ עֵינַ֔י at 14:29.

primary_reviews.rationale: The near edge is solid, carried by the altar notice, the pe after 14:35 and a new proposal at 14:36. Everything else about the high grade is in trouble. Count the speech formulas inside and around this span: 14:36 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֡וּל, 14:38 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל, 14:40 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר with no subject at all, 14:41 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֗וּל, 14:42 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל, and then 14:43 וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שָׁאוּל֙. Six occurrences of one formula, and the draft cuts after the fifth. Nothing distinguishes the sixth from the fifth, and the closing clause makes it worse rather than better: the span ends וַיִּלָּכֵ֖ד יוֹנָתָֽן, which repeats the wording already used one verse earlier at 14:41, וַיִּלָּכֵ֧ד יוֹנָתָ֛ן וְשָׁא֖וּל. A boundary whose terminus repeats its own penultimate clause and whose marker is the fifth of six identical formulas is not an evidenced edge. There is a second matter. The row describes a formal lot-casting narrowing step by step, but MT gives the oracle request as two words, הָ֣בָה תָמִ֑ים, which does not state the binary that the very next clause presupposes when it separates Jonathan and Saul from the people. Settling that lies outside what these sources allow, and I make no attempt; the reportable fact is that the procedure the row describes as formal is, in MT as printed, elliptical at its pivot.

primary_reviews.rationale: High confidence holds at both edges: the pursuit proposal opens against the prior summary-notice register (confirmed above), and v.42's terse 'Jonathan was selected' gives way at v.43 to a direct, personal interrogation ('Tell me what you have done!') -- an impersonal procedural notice yielding to face-to-face confrontation, a clean shift. It is worth naming explicitly that this is the second of three narrowing/elimination type-scenes within this reviewer's own assigned range: the royal lot at 10:20-24 (tribe to family to man), this guilt-lot at 14:36-42 (all Israel to Saul-and-Jonathan to Jonathan), and the parade-elimination that will follow at 16:6-10 (Jesse's sons eliminated one by one). The unit's internal cohesion is also good: Samuel's question at 15:14 turns on קֽוֹל הַצֹּ֥אן, and Saul's answer at 15:15 supplies מֵיטַ֤ב הַצֹּאן֙ with the חמל root that reaches back to the command at 15:3, so accusation and evasion are lexically interlocked. One item the record should carry: 15:16 shows ויאמרו in the text with וַיֹּ֥אמֶר to be read, the same singular-against-plural situation that arises at 12:5, where the drafted rationale took the plural as the Hebrew's own reading. Two instances in one book make it worth a consistent policy rather than a case-by-case choice.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two faults, and both bear on the high. The far edge first. This span opens וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שָׁא֤וּל אֶל שְׁמוּאֵל֙ חָטָ֔אתִי at 15:24 and the draft ends it at 15:29, immediately before 15:30, which reads וַיֹּ֣אמֶר חָטָ֔אתִי. The seam is therefore marked by the same verb and the same confession word that open the unit, with the subject not even expressed the second time, so it has to be retrieved from inside the span the boundary is supposed to close. That is symmetric marking at its most acute, and neither witness places a mark at 15:29; the nearest samekh falls after 15:26, span-internal, where Samuel's refusal ends and the robe-tearing begins. The second fault is a misattribution. The row traces the tension at 15:29 back to the prophet's sleepless grief, but what 15:11 gives Samuel is וַיִּ֨חַר֙ לִשְׁמוּאֵ֔ל וַיִּזְעַ֥ק, two entirely different roots. The נחם at 15:11 is spoken by Yahweh about himself, נִחַ֗מְתִּי. The irony the row is reaching for is real and worth keeping, but it runs from Yahweh's own נחם at 15:11 through its denial at 15:29 to its reassertion at 15:35, and Samuel's anger is not part of it.

The torn-robe sign-act itself (gesture plus interpreting word delivered as one event) is a recognized prophetic sign-act pattern, and keeping it fused with its verbal pronouncement rather than splitting act from speech is correct.

primary_reviews.rationale: This closes the נחם inclusio and the high rating is more than earned. v.35's נִחָ֔ם (Niphal perfect third-masculine-singular) is confirmed as the same root and binyan family as v.11's נִחַ֗מְתִּי and v.29's יִנָּחֵ֑ם/לְהִנָּחֵֽם -- a real, three-point grammatical inclusio, not a loose thematic echo. The closing edge into 16:1 is stronger than a simple genre-and-formula shift: 16:1's 'How long will you mourn for Saul' directly answers, in vocabulary, 15:35's 'Samuel mourned for Saul' -- the new unit's opening line responds to the closed unit's final image rather than merely following it. That kind of explicit lexical hand-off across a boundary is a sophisticated confirmatory device in Hebrew narrative (new pericopes often open by picking up a key term from what just closed) and it strengthens, rather than merely coexists with, the formal/genre shift into direct divine speech that already justifies the edge on its own.

primary_reviews.rationale: The successive-rejection type-scene is well-bounded at its open (confirmed above) and, within this reviewer's assigned range, cleanly closes at v.10's summary of the seventh rejection -- the sequence's actual resolution (v.11 onward) falls outside the delivered decisions and is not assessed here. Keeping the 'man looks at the outward appearance' saying (v.7) embedded in the sequence rather than isolated as a free-standing maxim is correct: it is Yahweh's direct, situationally-triggered answer to Samuel's specific misjudgment of Eliab, not detached wisdom material. This closes out a structural observation worth stating plainly as this cluster's capstone finding: this reviewer's assigned range (chs. 9-16) contains three deliberate narrowing/elimination type-scenes -- the tribal lot at 10:20-24, the guilt-lot at 14:36-42, and this parade-elimination at 16:6-10 -- each isolating one man from a larger field by a different mechanism (sacred lot twice, visual parade once) but sharing the identical narrative shape of successive elimination toward a single chosen or guilty individual. Recognizing that three-fold pattern is available evidence that the segmentation across this whole stretch of the book is tracking a real, intentional structural device rather than imposing one, and it should be weighed as corroboration across all three spans, not only this one.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold on original-language grounds. The unit opens where Samuel breaks off the parade of sons to ask whether they are finished, and it shuts with an itinerary clause, wayyaqom shemu'el wayyelekh haramatah, which is the ordinary Hebrew way of clearing a scene. Between them stands the anointing plus the Spirit's rushing (wattitslach ruach YHWH el dawid), so the type-scene reaches its stated resolution inside the span. The drafter's appeal to appearance-vocabulary reused from the preceding refusal is fair: v.12 recycles the very look-at terms v.7 had just discounted. A samekh stands after 16:13 in both section witnesses, which is weak Prophets-grade corroboration of the closing edge and nothing more. I note without treating it as counter-evidence that a pe falls after 16:12, i.e. between the two verses the draft binds most tightly; the content link there (Arise, anoint him -> then Samuel took the horn) is strong enough that I would not disturb the span.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold. The opening send-for formula answers Samuel's own question two verses earlier ("Are all your children here?"), and the close is doubly marked: the narrative supplies its own resolution formula ("Yahweh's Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward") and then a location-change notice ("Samuel rose up and went to Ramah") that this book uses repeatedly to seal a completed episode before pivoting elsewhere -- the same device closes the Naioth crisis at 19:24 and, on the Hebrew side of the chapter boundary, launches the very next unit at what MT numbers 21:1. Read as a type-scene, this is a deliberate structural rhyme with Saul's own elevation narrative in ch.9-10: both kings are found only after the obvious candidates are exhausted and the least-likely one is fetched from manual labor (donkeys/sheep) on someone else's prompting. The rejected alternative correctly isolates the anointing as the type-scene's climax rather than folding it into the refusal sequence; I would only add that the tonal break the rationale cites (repeated refusal to unqualified command) is reinforced by a syntactic break too -- every prior candidate is dismissed in the narrator's or Samuel's voice, but v.12's imperative comes directly from Yahweh, the first direct-speech intervention in the whole audition sequence.

primary_reviews.rationale: The unit is a coherent proposal-and-candidate scene, and the boundary at v.18 (before Saul actually sends) is sound. Worth flagging for the record: the courtier's commendation in v.18 is strikingly over-informed for a servant who has never seen David fight -- "a mighty man of valor, a man of war" anticipates the Goliath episode by a full chapter, and "prudent in speech" anticipates the résumé speech David has not yet given Saul. This is not a boundary problem, but it is a genuine narrative-grammar feature the rationale does not name: the servant functions here as a proleptic narrator-surrogate, and the resulting dramatic-irony gap (Saul hearing a full character reference for a man he has not yet met) is part of what makes his failure to recognize David at 17:55-58 land as strange rather than simply careless. The rejected alternative's reasoning (both speeches jointly propose and supply the candidate) holds; splitting at v.16/17 would sever a single persuasive move into diagnosis-without-remedy and remedy-without-diagnosis.

primary_reviews.rationale: Codepoint comparison places both Hebrew citations exactly within their verses, and the three WEB quotations match the substrate apart from straight-for-curly apostrophes. The rear edge also survives a check I made specifically because the WEB verse runs long: MT 17:51 itself ends with וַיִּרְא֧וּ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֛ים כִּֽי מֵ֥ת גִּבּוֹרָ֖ם וַיָּנֻֽסוּ, so the flight notice the row closes on is inside verse 51 in both witnesses and no versification slippage is involved. Disclosing the doublet rather than smoothing it, while declining to move the edges, is the right outcome, and high-to-medium matches the acknowledged internal tension. The front-edge Hebrew is transliterated but not quoted as an oshb ref.

Verified oshb 17:50-17:51 and WEB 17:48/17:50/17:51 citations exact -- including confirming, after correcting my own initial parser (which had dropped a mid-verse WEB paragraph continuation), that 'When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled' is indeed part of WEB's own v.51, not a separate verse. The internal doublet the row discloses is precisely verified: 17:50 uses the Hifil 'vayemitehu' (he killed him) with 'no sword in David's hand,' while 17:51 uses the Polel 'vayemotetehu' (a different causative form of the same mem-vav-tav root) after David takes Goliath's own sword -- an honest disclosure of real internal tension without moving the edges.

primary_reviews.rationale: Three separate faults, in a decision rated high. The span is 18:6-9 but the evidence refs are 18:7 and 18:9, so the opening edge is uncited and unargued - the rationale never says why v.6, which brings the women out of the cities, opens the unit rather than closing the homecoming. The irony is that the opening edge is easily supported: v.6 begins wayehi bevo'am, a temporal anchor of the same shape as v.1's, and a pe stands after 18:5. Second, the literature_type call is poetic_refrain for a four-verse span of which three verses are ordinary narrative; the couplet occupies v.7 alone. Third, the stated warrant for the poetry is the source text's q-line markers, which is translation formatting, and the same markup system separates v.8 from the couplet - so if it were allowed to drive anything it would drive against this span. The couplet is genuinely poetic on Hebrew grounds, hikkah sha'ul ... wedawid berivvotaw, a tight bicolon with matched constituents and a numerical escalation; that is the evidence to cite. The closing edge at v.9 is fine and has a samekh.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the most consequential decision in my range and it is under-specified in a way that matters to the whole packet. The crosswalk records chapter 20 as identical, 42 verses against 42, and that count-level verdict conceals a real content offset at the chapter's last verse. In the Hebrew, 20:42 ends at 'ad 'olam; the clause that the translation carries as the second half of 20:42 - he arose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city - is a separate verse in the Masoretic text, and it is 21:1. That is where the chapter-21 dual-citation offset originates. This span therefore closes across a numbering seam, carries no dual citation, and says nothing about it, while the next four decisions dual-cite a discrepancy that begins here. Separately, the claim that the signal was enacted exactly as planned is false in a way the Hebrew makes sharp. The edges themselves I would keep.

primary_reviews.rationale: The signal enactment and farewell are correctly bound together by the boy's ignorance-versus-the-pair's-knowledge contrast the rationale names, and closing on the parting is a defensible literary reading of v.42 on WEB's own terms. But the rationale's specific claim -- that this decision "closes the whole covenant sequence and the chapter on their parting" -- does not disclose a genuine competing segmentation that the campaign's own working files independently support twice over. First, the crosswalk flags ch.21 as mt_extra_1 (16 MT verses against 15 WEB verses); second, and more specifically, I checked the oshb text directly: oshb 1Sam.20.42 contains only the oath's content through "forever," and the clause WEB prints as the back half of v.42 -- "He arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city" -- is oshb 1Sam.21.1, i.e. the Masoretic tradition's own chapter division launches ch.21 with David's departure motion rather than closing ch.20 with it. That is corroborated a third way: the parashah two-witness pe marker for this stretch falls after MT 20:42, meaning the Masoretic paragraphing itself treats the oath's conclusion ("forever") as the break-point and reads "he arose and went" as belonging with what follows, not what precedes. Two independent structural signals (chapter division and paragraph marking) agree that this clause is at least as readable as the opening beat of the flight-and-Nob sequence as it is the closing coda of the farewell -- a genuine alternative segmentation the rationale never surfaces, on a decision that sits on a chapter (20, marked "identical" in the crosswalk) whose own final verse is the exact mechanism producing ch.21's extra-verse status. I am not asking for the WEB-based span to be redrawn, since WEB's own verse and chapter numbering is the citation register this campaign uses; I am asking that the rationale disclose the rival Hebrew segmentation the same way the campaign already discloses LXX-shorter-text seams and dual-citation chapters elsewhere in this range.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the most careful versification work in my assignment and it holds up under independent reconstruction. I verified from OSHB that MT 20:42 ends at עַד עוֹלָֽם and that וַיָּ֖קָם וַיֵּלַ֑ךְ וִיהוֹנָתָ֖ן בָּ֥א הָעִֽיר is a separate verse, MT 21:1, while my re-parse of the WEB pilcrow layer shows both stretches inside a single WEB 20:42 — so the dual citation WEB 20:42 = MT 20:42 + MT 21:1 is exactly right, and the row is correct that chapter 20's 42/42 'identical' relation in the crosswalk is a count-level artifact concealing a content-level seam at the chapter's last verse, and that this is the mechanical origin of chapter 21's mt_extra_1 status. The pe placement inference is also right: the two-witness list sites a pe after MT 20:42, which therefore falls between the oath and the departure clause, inside WEB's merged verse, corroborating the MT break rather than the row's WEB-numbered edge — and the row says so rather than claiming it as support. The plan/enactment correction verifies at every point I tested: 20:20 plans שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת הַחִצִּ֖ים, 20:22 uses plural הַחִצִּ֖ים מִמְּךָ֣ וָהָ֑לְאָה, 20:36 and 20:37 both narrate singular הַחֵ֖צִי, and 20:38 carries ketiv החצי against qere הַ֣חִצִּ֔ים — singular written, plural read, precisely as claimed. Only a typographic note: the WEB 20:42 quotation elides the closing quote marks between 'forever.' and 'He arose', which is presentational, not substantive.

The most rigorously verified decision in the batch. Directly confirmed against web_mt_crosswalk.json that chapter 20 is count-identical (42/42) while chapter 21 is mt_extra_1 (15 WEB verses / 16 MT verses), exactly as cited. Directly confirmed by comparing oshb 1Sam.20.42 and 1Sam.21.1 against WEB's own printed text that WEB's v.42 literally concatenates MT 20:42 (ending 'ad olam') with MT 21:1 ('vayaqam vayelekh, vi-Yonatan ba ha'ir' = 'he arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city') -- the row's hypothesis about the mechanical origin of the chapter-21 verse offset is directly demonstrable from the two source files, not merely plausible. Also verified the arrow-count claim precisely: vv.20 and 22 use the plural 'hachitzim' (the arrows) for the plan, vv.36-37 use the singular 'hachetzi' (the arrow) for the enactment, and v.38 contains a genuine ketiv/qere pair (ketiv singular, qere plural) that preserves rather than resolves the discrepancy. pe after MT 20:42 confirmed at the disclosed location. Exemplary work.

primary_reviews.rationale: The most serious defect I found in clusters 13-18: the rationale contradicts its own span. It states that the unit closes on Ahimelech's protest of ignorance 'before the sentence is pronounced', and its rejected alternative locates the death sentence at vv.17-19. But the protest of ignorance is v.15, and the span runs to v.16 - and v.16 is the sentence: wayyomer hammelekh mot tamut 'achimelekh 'attah wekhol beit 'avikha, an infinitive-absolute death formula addressed to Ahimelech by name. What stands at vv.17-19 is the execution order to the runners and the massacre that follows, which is a different speech act. As written the decision cannot be evaluated: either the span is one verse too long or the rationale describes a different span. The boundary may well be right at v.16 - a sentence is a natural close - but that is not what the rationale argues.

The analogy to 9:9 is functional only; that gloss is built on לְפָנִים plus an explanatory frame and shares no construction with this verse. primary_reviews.rationale: The verse itself checks out as a retrospective aside supplying the ephod Abiathar carries into the following inquiry scenes. But the comparison drawn to the 9:9 gloss to justify keeping v.6 isolated overstates the resemblance between the two: 9:9 is a direct address to the reader explaining a change in terminology ('he who is now called a prophet was before called a Seer'), a genre apart from ordinary narration, while 23:6 is an ordinary flashback clause ('vayehi bivroach' -- 'and it happened, when X fled') of the kind used elsewhere in the book to backfill a detail before resuming the main sequence. Both supply background, but only one breaks the narrating voice to comment on language; treating them as the same 'kind' of unit risks implying 23:6 is authorial commentary when it is still narrated event, just told out of strict chronological order.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Jonathan visit itself (vv.16-18) is accurately described, and the 'third covenant' count is right -- this follows 18:3 and 20:16-17/20:42 as a third recorded Jonathan-David pact, a genuine and checkable pattern. But the span as drawn folds two different things together: vv.14-15 is a general summary of David's fugitive condition ('Saul sought him every day, but God didn't deliver him into his hand'; 'David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life'), and only v.16 opens the specific, dated Jonathan encounter ('Jonathan, Saul's son, arose and went to David into the woods'). primary_reviews.rationale: The pairing is probably correct and the Hebrew argues for it more forcefully than the record does: v.43 fronts its object (וְאֶת אֲחִינֹעַם לָקַח דָּוִד) and v.44 fronts its subject (וְשָׁאוּל נָתַן), so the two verses are a matched pair of suspended clauses, not merely two facts of the same kind. First, the type: a genealogical register needs a lineage chain or a begetting formula, and there is neither here - these are marital and annalistic notices about who took whom and who was given to whom. Second, and more serious for a row at high, the only alternative disposed of is the upward merge into the Abigail narrative, which the fronting already rules out. The alternative the evidence actually raises is a split between the two verses, and both paragraph witnesses put a samekh after MT 25:43, exactly there. primary_reviews.rationale: I accept the unit. The close is excellent - v.12 ends on a stacked explanatory chain, וְאֵין רֹאֶה וְאֵין יוֹדֵעַ וְאֵין מֵקִיץ כִּי כֻלָּם יְשֵׁנִים כִּי תַּרְדֵּמַת יְהוָה נָפְלָה עֲלֵיהֶם, and explanatory codas of that shape terminate episodes. What I cannot accept is the sentence used to reject the internal division, because the text contradicts it. The record says the refusal and the counter-proposal are one uninterrupted exchange; in fact the speech formula is doubled. v.9 has וַיֹּאמֶר דָּוִד אֶל אֲבִישַׁי and v.10 has a second וַיֹּאמֶר דָּוִד with no reply from Abishai in between. A re-introduced speaker who has not been answered is the classic marker of an internal join, and the chapter's heaviest Masoretic mark - a pe, in both witnesses - falls precisely between the two. The device is genuinely ambiguous and I would not redraw the span on it, but the record has staked a high rating on a claim of continuity that the text does not support.
